phases.title: Planning & Preparation
phases.description: Get organized before you start building

steps.title: Verify All Components
steps.description: Check that you have all required parts before starting
steps.content:
Lay out all your components and compare them against your build plan. This prevents mid-build delays and helps you understand what you're working with.

**What to verify:**
1. **Switches** - Count them. You need enough for both keyboard halves plus a few spares
2. **Microcontrollers** - Verify you have 2 (one for each half)
3. **Diodes** - Should match switch count (1N4148 through-hole or SMD)
4. **PCB or wiring materials** - PCB boards or 30AWG wire for handwiring
5. **Connectors** - TRRS jacks and cable for wired, or batteries for wireless
6. **Case components** - Plates, bottom plates, screws, standoffs
7. **Optional features** - RGB LEDs, OLED displays, rotary encoders if chosen
8. **Keycaps** - Verify correct profile and count

**Take photos** of your organized workspace - it helps when you need to remember where things are.
warnings: Missing components will delay your build by days or weeks
Verify microcontroller pin compatibility with your firmware choice before soldering
tips: Create a physical checklist and mark off items as you verify them
Test microcontrollers before soldering - flash a blink sketch to verify they work
Order 10-20% extra switches and diodes in case of failures

steps.title: Set Up Your Workspace
steps.description: Prepare a safe, organized workspace for building
steps.content:
A proper workspace makes building safer and more enjoyable. You'll be here for several hours, so get comfortable.

**Essential setup:**
1. **Work surface** - Clean, flat, well-lit table or desk. Use a cutting mat or silicone mat to protect the surface
2. **Lighting** - Bright overhead light plus a desk lamp for detail work. LED work lights are ideal
3. **Ventilation** - Soldering produces fumes. Work near a window or use a small fan to direct fumes away
4. **Organization** - Small containers or compartmented trays for sorting screws, diodes, resistors
5. **Reference materials** - Keep this guide, your build plan, and component datasheets accessible on a tablet or second monitor

**Comfort:**
- Adjustable chair at proper height
- Take breaks every 45-60 minutes
- Keep water nearby
- Have snacks ready for longer sessions
warnings: Never solder in an enclosed space without ventilation
Keep flammable materials away from soldering iron
Have a fire extinguisher nearby (kitchen ABC type is fine)
tips: Use anti-static mats or wrist straps when handling electronics
Label containers with painter's tape for easy identification
Take photos at each major step - helps with troubleshooting later

steps.title: Prepare Your Tools
steps.description: Gather and prepare all tools you'll need
steps.content:
Having all tools ready prevents workflow interruptions. Here's what you'll need based on your build method.

**Universal tools (all builds):**
- Soldering iron (60W temperature-controlled recommended, 300-350°C for electronics)
- Solder (60/40 or 63/37 rosin core, 0.8mm diameter)
- Flush cutters for trimming component leads
- Tweezers (fine-tipped for SMD work)
- Multimeter for continuity testing
- USB cable (USB-C or Micro-USB depending on controller)

**Handwired builds add:**
- Wire strippers (for 30AWG wire)
- 30AWG solid core wire (multiple colors for rows/columns)
- Helping hands or PCB holder
- Diagonal cutters

**PCB builds add:**
- Solder wick or desoldering pump (for mistakes)
- Flux pen
- Isopropyl alcohol (90%+) and brush for cleaning

**Testing tools:**
- Keyboard testing website (bookmark: keyboardchecker.com)
- Firmware flashing software ready to install

**Prepare your soldering iron:**
1. Clean the tip with brass wire or damp sponge
2. Tin the tip with fresh solder
3. Set temperature to 300-350°C (575-660°F)
4. Let it fully heat before starting work
warnings: Hot soldering irons can cause serious burns - always use a proper stand
Lead solder contains lead - wash hands after soldering, never eat while soldering
Keep soldering iron tip tinned to prevent oxidation
tips: Buy a temperature-controlled iron if you plan to build more keyboards - it's worth it
Keep a damp sponge or brass wire tip cleaner handy and clean often
If you've never soldered, practice on scrap wire first

steps.title: Review Your Build Strategy
steps.description: Understand the assembly sequence before starting
steps.content:
Take 15 minutes to read through all the steps ahead. This helps you understand the workflow and spot potential issues before they become problems.

**Understanding your build path:**
Your build method determines your assembly approach. Review the steps specific to your choice:

- **Handwired:** You'll wire the switch matrix manually, giving maximum flexibility but requiring careful planning
- **Custom PCB:** You designed the PCB, so you'll solder components to it following your schematic
- **PCB Kit:** The PCB is pre-designed, making assembly straightforward - just follow the kit instructions

**Build order overview:**
1. Build the key matrix (switches + diodes)
2. Connect the microcontroller
3. Add optional features (RGB, OLED, encoders)
4. Flash firmware
5. Test every key
6. Final assembly into case

**Common first-time mistakes to avoid:**
- Soldering controller before testing matrix
- Wrong diode orientation (very common!)
- Forgetting to test before case assembly
- Flashing wrong firmware for controller type

**Time management:**
Plan for these approximate times:
- Matrix assembly: 3-8 hours (depends on method)
- Wiring controller: 1-2 hours
- Firmware setup: 1-3 hours (first time)
- Testing and troubleshooting: 1-2 hours
- Case assembly: 30-60 minutes

Don't rush. Taking your time prevents expensive mistakes.
tips: Read all warnings in red before starting each phase
Bookmark this page or save the PDF for offline reference
Join the keyboard building Discord communities - they're helpful for real-time questions

steps.title: Set up the KiCad project
steps.description: Install KiCad 8+, install keyboard footprint libraries (ai03 MX, marbastlib for Choc), and create the project skeleton.
steps.content:
KiCad is the standard tool for keyboard PCB design. Spend the time to set it up properly once and reuse the same footprint libraries across every future board.

**Install KiCad:**
1. Download KiCad 8 or newer from https://www.kicad.org/download/. Linux: prefer the official PPA (`sudo add-apt-repository ppa:kicad/kicad-8.0-releases`) over distro packages
2. On first launch, accept the default global symbol/footprint paths
3. Verify by running `kicad --version` from a terminal

**Install keyboard footprint libraries:**
KiCad ships with general-purpose libraries but no keyboard-specific footprints. The two libraries you almost certainly need are:

- **ai03 MX library** — Cherry MX and clones, hot-swap variants. https://github.com/ai03-2725/MX_Alps_Hybrid
- **marbastlib** — Kailh Choc v1 / v2, low-profile footprints. https://github.com/ebastler/marbastlib

Clone both into a libraries directory you control:
```
mkdir -p ~/kicad-libs && cd ~/kicad-libs
git clone https://github.com/ai03-2725/MX_Alps_Hybrid.git
git clone https://github.com/ebastler/marbastlib.git
```

In KiCad: **Preferences → Manage Symbol Libraries → Project Specific Libraries → +** and add the `.kicad_sym` files. Repeat in **Manage Footprint Libraries** for the `.pretty` directories.

**Create the project:**
1. **File → New → Project** — pick a directory and a name (e.g. `mysplit-v1`). KiCad creates a folder with `.kicad_pro`, `.kicad_sch`, `.kicad_pcb` files
2. Initialise git in that folder (`git init && git add . && git commit -m "Initial project"`) — every revision of a PCB design should be tracked, especially before sending Gerbers to a fab
3. Open the schematic editor (the leftmost icon)

**Decide MX vs Choc before drawing anything:**
The footprint dictates the physical pad layout, switch spacing, and case keep-out areas. Switching footprint libraries mid-design forces you to re-place every switch.
- **MX (19.05mm × 19.05mm grid)** — standard mechanical, most keycap options, taller
- **Choc v1 (18mm × 17mm grid)** — low-profile, shorter, less keycap variety
- **Choc v2** — a hybrid; uses MX-like keycap stems with low-profile housings

Write your decision into the project README so future-you remembers.
tips: Pin the project libraries to a fixed git commit — silent footprint updates upstream can break clearances on a board you already sent to fab
KiCad project paths are stored relative to the .kicad_pro file when you use ${KIPRJMOD} — use that prefix so the project is portable across machines
completionCriteria: KiCad opens the project from a fresh terminal session
Footprint browser shows MX and Choc footprints under your custom libraries
Project directory is under git version control

steps.title: Draw the schematic (matrix + controller)
steps.description: Place switch symbols, one diode per key, the controller footprint, TRRS jack, reset button, and net the rows and columns.
steps.content:
The schematic captures the electrical relationships before any physical layout decisions. Get it right here and the layout becomes mechanical work.

**Matrix wiring — the core idea:**
A keyboard matrix is rows × columns of switches with a diode at each intersection. The controller scans by driving one row line at a time and reading which column lines are pulled low. The diode prevents current from flowing backward and creating "ghost" key presses when three or more keys are pressed simultaneously.

**Diode direction matters and must match the firmware:**
- **`COL2ROW`** (most QMK builds) — diode anode on the column side, cathode (stripe) on the row side
- **`ROW2COL`** — opposite

Pick one before placing any diodes. The QMK config (`config.h`: `#define DIODE_DIRECTION COL2ROW`) and the schematic must agree, or every key will read as the wrong key (or nothing).

**Place per-switch units:**
For each physical key:
1. Place an `SW_Push` symbol (or the keyboard-specific switch symbol if your library provides one)
2. Place a `D` diode adjacent to it
3. Wire one switch terminal to the diode anode, the other terminal to a column net (`Col0`, `Col1`, ...)
4. Wire the diode cathode to a row net (`Row0`, `Row1`, ...)

Use global labels named `Row0`...`RowN` and `Col0`...`ColN` so you do not need to draw long wires across the schematic. Hierarchical sheets are useful once you exceed ~30 keys.

**Controller block:**
Place your controller symbol (Pro Micro, Elite-C, nice!nano, RP2040). Wire each row net and each column net to a GPIO pin. Note the assignment in a comment — you will need this exact mapping in the QMK matrix definition.
- VCC → 5V or 3.3V depending on controller
- GND → matrix common ground
- Reset pin → through a tactile switch to GND, with a 100nF cap from RST to GND for noise rejection

**TRRS jack (wired splits):**
4 contacts — `Tip`, `Ring1`, `Ring2`, `Sleeve`. Typical wiring for split halves:
- Tip → Data (D+ for serial, SCL for I2C)
- Ring1 → second data line (D- or SDA)
- Ring2 → VCC (5V from master half)
- Sleeve → GND

Add two ESD protection diodes (e.g. PESD3V3L4UF) on the data lines and a 10kΩ pull-up on each — TRRS plugs short pins as they are inserted, which can latch up the controller.

**Optional features (only if your build includes them):**
- **RGB LEDs** — daisy-chain WS2812B/SK6812. One data line from a free GPIO, VCC = 5V, GND. Add a 470Ω resistor in series with the data line and a 1000μF cap across VCC/GND near the first LED
- **OLED** — 4 pins (VCC, GND, SCL, SDA). Wire to the controller I2C pins. The display itself is socketed on the PCB later
- **Encoder** — 5 pins (A, B, common, switch, switch-common). A and B go to two GPIOs, common to GND, switch to a third GPIO with the switch-common to GND

**Annotate and run ERC:**
1. **Tools → Annotate Schematic** — assigns reference designators (D1, D2, SW1, SW2, ...)
2. **Inspect → Electrical Rules Checker** — must pass with zero errors. Common issues: unconnected pins (add `no-connect` flags on intentionally unused MCU pins), driver conflicts (two outputs on one net)
warnings: If diode orientation in the schematic does not match the firmware's DIODE_DIRECTION, the matrix will not work correctly even if every solder joint is perfect
tips: Save the controller pin → row/column mapping as a comment block in the schematic. You will paste it into the QMK matrix definition later
Number rows and columns in the same order you scan them physically — left-to-right, top-to-bottom — to make debugging easier
completionCriteria: Every switch has a diode in the correct orientation
Every row and column has a global label connecting it to a controller GPIO
ERC passes with zero errors and only intentional warnings

steps.title: Assign footprints
steps.description: Map each schematic symbol to a physical footprint (PCB land pattern). The schematic is electrical; the footprint is geometry.
steps.content:
Footprint assignment is where the schematic becomes a physical board. KiCad does not infer footprints from symbols — every part needs an explicit assignment.

**Open the assignment tool:**
**Tools → Assign Footprints** in the schematic editor. The dialog lists every component on the left and available footprints in the middle/right.

**Switches — the most consequential choice:**
Pick consciously between four common variants:
- **MX, soldered, 3-pin** — `MX_Alps_Hybrid:MXOnly-1U-NoLED` — cheapest, only 3 pads (no PCB-mount stabilising posts)
- **MX, soldered, 5-pin** — `MX_Alps_Hybrid:MXOnly-1U` — adds two plastic-post holes for stability
- **MX, hot-swap** — `MX_Alps_Hybrid:MX-Hotswap-1U` — Kailh socket on the back side, switch inserts from the front. Required if you want tool-less switch swapping
- **Choc v1 hot-swap** — `marbastlib-choc:CHOC_V1_1U_HOTSWAP` — equivalent for low-profile builds

Mixing soldered and hot-swap on the same board is fine and sometimes useful (hot-swap for the alphas, soldered for thumb keys to save space).

**Diodes — through-hole vs SMD:**
- **Through-hole** — `Diode_THT:D_DO-35_SOD27_P7.62mm_Horizontal` — easy to solder, takes more board space, ugly under low-profile keycaps
- **SMD SOD-123** — `Diode_SMD:D_SOD-123` — compact, tucks under switch, harder to solder by hand but doable with flux + tweezers

For a first PCB, through-hole is more forgiving. Once you have soldered SMD on something else, switch.

**Controller footprint — choose by mounting style:**
- **Pro Micro / Elite-C edge-mounted** — board has a rectangular cutout, controller solders in flush. Saves vertical space but the pinout is fixed
- **Pro Micro on headers** — sockets the controller, lets you replace if it dies. Standard for first builds
- **Direct-solder Pro Micro footprint on top of the PCB** — cheapest, but the USB connector then sits proud of the board

The socketed-on-headers footprint is usually `Pro_Micro:Pro_Micro_Sockets`. Make sure the footprint matches your physical headers (round Mill-Max sockets vs square pin headers) — pad spacing differs.

**TRRS jack — confirm part number:**
The most common is `Connector_Audio:Jack_3.5mm_PJ320A`. Cheap clones from AliExpress sometimes use a slightly different footprint — check pad spacing against the physical part with calipers before ordering.

**Run the netlist update:**
After assigning footprints, open the PCB editor (**Tools → Switch to PCB Editor** or open the `.kicad_pcb` file) and **Tools → Update PCB from Schematic**. KiCad imports every part as a footprint into the layout area. They start in a pile in one corner — placement comes next.
tips: The footprint browser (Footprint Editor → File → Browse Library) shows the actual pad geometry — preview before assigning
When the same diode appears 60 times, assign once and use the right-pane "apply to all components with same value" — saves 59 clicks
completionCriteria: Every component in the schematic has a footprint assigned (no warnings about missing footprints)
Switch and diode footprints match the parts you actually have in hand

steps.title: Lay out the PCB
steps.description: Place switches per the keyboard layout, route copper, add silkscreen, define the board edge.
steps.content:
Layout is the longest single step in a custom PCB project. The goal is a board where every component sits where it must, no traces cross, and the edge cuts match what your case expects.

**Start from a layout file, not from scratch:**
Most split keyboards begin life as a Keyboard Layout Editor (http://www.keyboard-layout-editor.com) JSON file or an Ergogen YAML. Both can be converted to a KiCad PCB skeleton:
- **KLE → KiCad** — use https://github.com/adamws/keyboard-tools or `kbplacer` (https://github.com/adamws/kbplacer) to read a KLE JSON and place every switch footprint at the correct coordinates with one click
- **Ergogen** — generates a `.kicad_pcb` with switches and outlines already placed; you import diodes/controller manually after

If you place switches by hand, work in 1U increments (19.05mm MX, 18mm Choc) and use the **Edit → Move Exactly** dialog with absolute coordinates. Eyeballing leaves keycap collisions you only discover after etching.

**Group placement:**
For each switch, place its diode within ~5mm and on the same layer. A common pattern for through-hole diodes:
- Diode body sits between two adjacent switches on the row axis
- Cathode pad is closer to the row trace, anode pad is closer to the column trace

For SMD diodes, tuck them between the two PCB-mount post holes on the back side of each switch — invisible from the top, no extra board area.

**Routing — single-layer vs two-layer:**
If your fabrication target is a fab house (JLCPCB), routing on two layers (rows on F.Cu, columns on B.Cu, vias to switch) is straightforward.

If you are etching at home with a laser, you almost certainly want **single-layer with jumpers**:
- Route everything you can on one copper layer (usually B.Cu)
- Where a row and column would cross, leave a gap and add a wire jumper or a 0Ω resistor on top
- Resist the urge to do double-sided home etching as a first project — alignment is the failure mode that wastes the most boards

**Trace width and clearance:**
- **Fab house (JLCPCB-style):** trace width 0.25mm, clearance 0.2mm is well within tolerance
- **Laser isolation:** trace width 0.4mm minimum, clearance 0.4mm minimum. The laser kerf and the resist edge raggedness eat ~0.15mm on each side

Set defaults in **File → Board Setup → Design Rules → Net Classes** before routing.

**Edge cuts — define the board outline:**
Use the **Edge.Cuts** layer. Common shapes:
- Rectangular for plate-mount cases
- Following the key layout outline for plateless / sandwich cases
- Rounded corners (1-3mm fillet) — sharper corners chip during V-cutting at the fab

Add at least 4 mounting holes (M2 or M3) at the corners and standoff positions defined by your case. KiCad: place a `MountingHole` footprint or draw a circle on Edge.Cuts.

**Silkscreen — version, name, orientation markers:**
- Board name and revision (e.g. `MYSPLIT v1.2`) on F.Silkscreen — front-facing and obvious
- A small triangle or dot indicating diode orientation near the first diode footprint — pays for itself the first time you assemble in low light
- A "L" / "R" mark indicating which half of the split this PCB is
- USB / TRRS connector labels

**Mirroring for the second half:**
Most split keyboards use the same PCB for both halves, with the controller socketed on the underside of one and the topside of the other. Verify your design supports this before sending to fab — it cuts your PCB cost in half.
requiredTools: Layout source (KLE JSON or Ergogen YAML)
warnings: Two-layer home etching is significantly harder than single-layer with jumpers. If this is your first PCB, do single-layer.
V-cut and routed corners on a fab board chip if the radius is below 0.5mm. Round corners explicitly.
tips: Place the controller, TRRS, and reset button first. They have fixed mechanical positions; switches have flexibility
Use the 3D viewer (Alt+3) regularly to check for component collisions and case fit
completionCriteria: Every net is routed (no unrouted ratlines visible)
No clearance violations at the chosen design rules
3D view matches the case envelope
Edge.Cuts forms a single closed polygon

steps.title: Run DRC and ERC
steps.description: Run the Design Rules Check and Electrical Rules Check before exporting any fabrication files.
steps.content:
DRC and ERC are your last automated catch before money or copper-clad is on the line. Treat any violation as a board you would have to scrap.

**Set the rules to match your fabrication target:**
Open **File → Board Setup → Design Rules → Constraints** and **→ Net Classes**.

**For a fab house (JLCPCB / PCBWay defaults):**
- Minimum trace width: 0.15mm (you should be using ≥0.25mm)
- Minimum clearance: 0.15mm (use ≥0.2mm)
- Minimum drill size: 0.3mm
- Minimum annular ring: 0.13mm

**For laser isolation routing (home):**
- Minimum trace width: 0.4mm
- Minimum clearance: 0.4mm (this is the critical one — the laser cannot reliably cut a thin gap)
- Drill diameters: round to whatever bit sizes you actually have (commonly 0.8mm and 1.0mm)

**Run DRC:**
**Inspect → Design Rules Checker → Run DRC**. Common findings:
- **Clearance violation** — a trace or pad is too close to another. Re-route or move
- **Unconnected items** — a net was supposed to be routed but is not. Check the ratsnest (the white "rubber band" lines)
- **Hole-to-hole clearance** — two through-holes are touching. Most common with closely-packed diode pads
- **Footprint courtyard overlap** — two parts physically overlap. Means the case will not assemble

Fix every error. Warnings — read each one and decide; do not blanket-ignore.

**Run ERC again on the schematic:**
Layout edits sometimes change net assignments (e.g. you re-routed a wire and inadvertently broke a net). Re-running ERC catches this.

**Run the connectivity check:**
**Inspect → Show Board Statistics → Connectivity** — confirms every net in the netlist has at least one segment of copper. A net with zero copper is silently broken.

**Visual sanity passes:**
- Toggle each layer on/off (`Alt+number`) — confirm no surprises (a stray polygon on F.Cu, an annotation on the wrong layer)
- 3D view — rotate and look for components clipping through the case outline
- Front and back render — confirm silkscreen is on the right side and not mirrored

**Check fabrication-house specific rules:**
If you are sending to JLCPCB, run their online "DRC" check after uploading the Gerbers — they catch things KiCad does not (panelisation tabs, V-cut clearance, fiducial placement on assembled boards). Do this BEFORE paying.
completionCriteria: DRC passes with zero errors
ERC passes with zero errors
Every net is fully connected (zero unrouted)
Visual scan of each layer shows nothing out of place

steps.title: Export Gerbers for a fab house
steps.description: Generate the standard set of Gerber files (copper, mask, silkscreen, edge) for JLCPCB / PCBWay / OSHPark.
steps.content:
Gerbers are the de facto industry standard for PCB fabrication. Every fab house accepts them; the only variation is which subset of layers to include and whether to ZIP them.

**Open the plot dialog:**
**File → Plot** (in the PCB editor).

**Layers to enable for a typical 2-layer keyboard PCB:**
- `F.Cu` — front copper
- `B.Cu` — back copper
- `F.Mask` — front soldermask (where copper is exposed)
- `B.Mask` — back soldermask
- `F.Silkscreen` — front silkscreen text/graphics
- `B.Silkscreen` — back silkscreen
- `F.Paste` — front solder paste stencil (only if you are getting an SMT stencil)
- `B.Paste` — back solder paste stencil
- `Edge.Cuts` — board outline

Do not enable courtyard, fabrication, or comment layers — fab houses ignore them at best, get confused at worst.

**Plot format settings:**
- **Plot format:** Gerber (not PostScript, PDF, etc.)
- **Output directory:** create a `gerbers/` subfolder in your project
- **Use Protel filename extensions:** ON for OSHPark, OFF (use `.gbr`) for JLCPCB and PCBWay. Check the fab house docs
- **Generate Gerber job file:** ON (the `.gbrjob` describes the layer stack-up)
- **Subtract soldermask from silkscreen:** ON (prevents silk under exposed pads)
- **Use extended X2 format:** ON for modern fabs (JLCPCB, PCBWay), OFF only for legacy fabs that explicitly do not support X2

Click **Plot**.

**Generate drill files in the same dialog:**
Click **Generate Drill Files** at the bottom of the Plot dialog. See the next step for drill-specific settings.

**ZIP for upload:**
Most fabs require a single ZIP containing all Gerbers + drill files at the top level (no subdirectory). From a terminal:
```
cd gerbers
zip mysplit-v1-gerbers.zip *.gbr *.drl *.gbrjob
```

**Verify before paying:**
Upload the ZIP to the fab house portal — they all show a render of what they will manufacture. Check:
- Board outline matches your edge cuts
- Soldermask exposes the right pads
- Silkscreen is on the side you expect and is readable
- Drill holes appear in every position you expect
- Layer count matches what you ordered (a 2-layer order with 4 copper layer files will be flagged)

If the render looks wrong, it will manufacture wrong. Stop, fix in KiCad, re-export.
requiredTools: Account at JLCPCB / PCBWay / OSHPark / preferred fab
tips: Save the exact plot settings as a project preset — every revision should use identical settings to avoid surprise differences
Diff the new Gerber ZIP against the previous revision before ordering. https://gerber-viewer.ucamco.com renders side by side
completionCriteria: gerbers/ directory contains the expected layer files plus a .drl file
Fab house preview matches your KiCad 3D render
No layer count or layer naming warnings from the fab portal

steps.title: Export drill files
steps.description: Generate Excellon drill files (.drl) — required by fab houses, used by FlatCAM/pcb2gcode for through-hole drilling.
steps.content:
Excellon is the standard format for drill data. KiCad generates it from the same Plot dialog as Gerbers.

**Open the dialog:**
**File → Fabrication Outputs → Drill Files** (or click **Generate Drill Files** at the bottom of the Plot dialog).

**Settings for a fab house:**
- **Drill file format:** Excellon
- **Mirror Y axis:** OFF
- **Minimal header:** OFF (the fab wants the full header)
- **PTH and NPTH in single file:** OFF — produce two files. PTH = plated through-holes (vias, switch pins). NPTH = non-plated (mounting holes for screws)
- **Oval holes drill mode:** Use route command (G00)
- **Map file format:** PDF (a human-readable map of every drill position, useful for the fab to sanity-check)
- **Drill origin:** Absolute (matches the Gerber origin)
- **Drill units:** Millimeters
- **Zeros format:** Decimal format (most modern Excellon parsers handle this; some older fab tools want "Suppress leading zeros")

Click **Generate Drill File**.

You should see at least:
- `mysplit-PTH.drl` — plated holes
- `mysplit-NPTH.drl` — non-plated holes (mounting holes)
- `mysplit-drl_map.pdf` — the visual drill map

**Settings for FlatCAM / pcb2gcode (laser or CNC):**
Same as above with one change: **Zeros format → Suppress leading zeros**. Older CAM toolchains crash on the decimal form.

For CNC milling, also produce a separate Excellon for each drill diameter — pcb2gcode can then assign each tool to the right drill size automatically.

**Verify the drill map:**
Open the PDF map. Every hole should:
- Appear at a position you expect (no orphan holes from a deleted footprint)
- Have a sensible drill diameter (no 0.1mm holes — that is a configuration error)
- Be labelled with a tool number that matches the count in the .drl file

If the map shows holes in the wrong place, re-check the Plot dialog drill origin setting. Mismatched origins between Gerber and Excellon mean the fab drills holes in the wrong locations.
completionCriteria: PTH and NPTH .drl files exist
Drill map PDF shows holes only where you expect them
No drill diameter is suspiciously small (<0.3mm) or large (>3mm)

steps.title: Plot SVG / PDF for laser isolation
steps.description: Export each copper layer as an SVG or PDF — the simplest input for many laser PCB workflows.
steps.content:
For laser etching at home, the lowest-friction path is a vector image of each copper layer that you load directly into LightBurn or Inkscape. SVG is the better choice — clean vectors, scales without aliasing, easy to inspect.

**Open the plot dialog:**
**File → Plot** in the PCB editor.

**Settings for a single-layer SVG (back copper, looking through the board):**
- **Plot format:** SVG
- **Output directory:** `laser/` subfolder
- **Layers:** select **only** `B.Cu`. Uncheck everything else
- **Plot border and title block:** OFF
- **Plot footprint values:** OFF
- **Plot footprint references:** OFF (silk and references should not appear in copper output)
- **Force plotting of invisible values/references:** OFF
- **Mirrored plot:** **ON** — when you look at the back layer through the top of the board, it appears mirrored. Mirror at export so the laser etches the correct side
- **Negative plot:** OFF (we want copper-to-keep as black, copper-to-remove as white. Inverting comes later if your laser software needs the opposite)
- **Plot reference designators:** OFF
- **Sketch pads on fab layers:** OFF
- **Use Aux origin:** OFF (use the page origin)

Click **Plot**.

**Export the front layer:**
Same dialog, deselect `B.Cu`, select `F.Cu`, **Mirrored plot: OFF** (front layer is already viewed from the front).

**Export an alignment / drill reference layer:**
For double-sided boards, you need registration marks the laser can find on both sides. Add them to your KiCad design as small (1mm) drill holes at three corners, then plot the **Edge.Cuts + drill positions** to a third SVG. This becomes your alignment template.

In KiCad: there is no direct "drill positions only" plot. Two options:
- Open the drill PDF map and screen-grab the alignment marks
- Add three named footprints (`AlignMark_TL`, `AlignMark_TR`, `AlignMark_BR`) on the F.Silkscreen layer; plot F.Silkscreen to SVG

**Verify in Inkscape before lasering:**
1. Open each SVG
2. Confirm the dimensions match your board outline (use the ruler)
3. Confirm no extraneous text/marks slipped through
4. Confirm the back-layer SVG is mirrored relative to the front (you should see "REV 1.2" reading backwards on B.Cu)
5. Save as a copy with a clear filename: `mysplit-v1-bcu-mirrored.svg`

**PDF as an alternative:**
If your laser software prefers PDF:
- Same plot dialog, **Plot format: PDF**
- Same layer/mirror settings
- One PDF per layer

PDF is harder to inspect for unexpected content; prefer SVG when possible.
warnings: Forgetting to mirror the B.Cu plot is the most common laser-PCB mistake. Etch the wrong-handed board and the controller will sit on the wrong side.
tips: Add a small visible "F" or "B" text in copper near the edge of each layer in KiCad. After exporting, you can confirm at a glance which file is which side.
Save the SVG export settings as a KiCad project preset — re-doing them every revision is where mistakes creep in
completionCriteria: F.Cu and B.Cu SVGs exist; B.Cu is mirrored
Visual inspection in Inkscape confirms correct content and dimensions
Alignment marks are visible on both files at identical absolute positions

steps.title: Export copper as a raster image (PNG)
steps.description: For laser engravers driven by a raster image (LightBurn, LaserGRBL): export each copper layer as a high-DPI PNG.
steps.content:
Some laser workflows want a raster bitmap rather than vectors — typically when you are using laser-printer toner transfer or when your laser controller only accepts images. The reliable path is **KiCad → SVG → Inkscape → high-DPI PNG**.

**Step 1 — Plot to SVG (per the previous step):**
Use the same SVG export procedure. The vector source preserves all detail; rasterising is one-shot.

**Step 2 — Open in Inkscape and prepare:**
1. **File → Open** the SVG
2. **Edit → Select All** (`Ctrl+A`)
3. **Object → Object Properties** — confirm dimensions match the physical board
4. **File → Document Properties → Page → Resize page to drawing or selection** — crops the page to just the artwork
5. (Optional) **Object → Fill and Stroke** — set fill to pure black, stroke to none. This guarantees the raster is binary and the laser does not waste passes on grey

**Step 3 — Export PNG at high DPI:**
1. **File → Export** (`Ctrl+Shift+E`)
2. **Export area:** Page
3. **Image size — DPI:** **1000 DPI** for diode lasers (50W and below). **2000+ DPI** for fibre or CO₂ lasers with smaller spot sizes
4. **Image size — Width/Height** — confirm these match the physical board dimensions in pixels (e.g. 100mm board × 1000 DPI = ~3937 pixels wide)
5. **Bit depth:** 1-bit (true black/white). Avoids any anti-aliasing
6. **Filename:** include the layer and orientation: `mysplit-v1-bcu-mirrored-1000dpi.png`
7. Click **Export**

**Step 4 — Invert if your workflow needs it:**
The convention varies:
- **Laser ablates the resist where the image is BLACK** (most LightBurn workflows) — keep copper as black
- **Laser ablates the resist where the image is WHITE** (some LaserGRBL setups) — invert the image. In Inkscape: `Filters → Color → Invert`. Or in GIMP: `Colors → Invert`

Name the inverted file explicitly: `mysplit-v1-bcu-mirrored-INVERTED.png`. Do not assume next-week-you will remember which convention.

**Step 5 — Drill mark layer:**
Export the alignment / drill positions as a separate raster. The laser will burn small registration dots first, then you align the copper-clad to them before the main pass. Same DPI as the copper layer so the coordinates match.

**Sanity checks before lasering:**
- Open the PNG in an image viewer and zoom to 1:1. Trace edges should be sharp and uniform — no jagged stair-stepping (means DPI is too low) and no grey halos (means anti-aliasing slipped through)
- Measure a known-width feature (e.g. a 1mm trace) using the image viewer ruler. Width in pixels ÷ DPI should equal the physical width in inches
- Open in your laser software and preview — confirm the work area dimensions match the physical board
tips: Diode lasers are noisy — features below 0.3mm get lost. Bump trace width to ≥0.5mm in KiCad before exporting if you have any 0.4mm traces
Export the PNG at the same physical scale as the laser will burn. Resizing in the laser software introduces interpolation artefacts
completionCriteria: PNG dimensions in pixels = board dimensions × DPI
Image is true 1-bit (no greys)
Filename clearly states layer, mirror state, and invert state

steps.title: Prepare the copper-clad board
steps.description: Sand, clean, and apply the resist layer your laser will burn or ablate.
steps.content:
The laser does not etch copper directly — it ablates a thin resist layer on top of the copper. Whatever the laser exposes will be eaten by the etchant in a later step. Resist preparation is where most home PCB attempts succeed or fail.

**Source the copper-clad board:**
- **FR4 + 1oz copper** — standard, ~35μm copper. Etches in 5-15 minutes
- **FR4 + 2oz copper** — twice as thick, useful for higher-current builds. Doubles etch time
- **Single-sided** vs **double-sided** — pick to match your design. Single-sided is significantly easier to align and etch
- Cut to size with a hacksaw, scoring tool, or paper cutter (for thin material). Leave 5-10mm border around the design for handling

**Surface prep — non-negotiable:**
Any oxide, oil, or fingerprint under the resist will lift during etching, leaving pinholes in your traces.

1. **Wet-sand** with 600-800 grit silicon carbide paper under running water. Sand until the entire surface is uniformly matte and pink-red. No mirror spots, no dark patches
2. **Rinse** with clean water
3. **Acetone wipe** with a lint-free cloth — removes any residual oils
4. **Final rinse** with isopropyl alcohol (IPA) — leaves the surface ready for resist
5. **Do not touch the copper with bare fingers** after this point. Hold the board by the edges only

**Apply the resist — three common methods:**

**Method 1 — Spray paint (easiest, most forgiving):**
1. Use cheap matte black spray paint (e.g. Rust-Oleum 2X). Thin coats are critical
2. Spray 3-4 light coats with 5-10 minutes between each, in a well-ventilated area or outdoors
3. Dry overnight (24h is safer; the paint cures, not just dries)
4. The laser will ablate the paint where the image is, exposing the copper. Etchant attacks only the exposed copper
5. Best for diode lasers and for first-time laser PCB makers

**Method 2 — Laser-printed toner transfer (no laser ablation, but worth knowing):**
Not a laser-engraver method — uses a regular laser printer + iron. Skip if you are committed to laser ablation.

**Method 3 — Photoresist + laser as UV source:**
1. Apply pre-sensitised photoresist board (sold as such) or coat raw copper with liquid photoresist in a darkroom
2. Use a UV laser (405nm or shorter) to expose the resist where the image is
3. Develop in sodium carbonate solution
4. Highest resolution but most equipment-dependent

**Drying and storage:**
- Allow the resist to fully cure before lasering. Spray paint that is touch-dry can still smudge under the laser head
- Store unused coated boards in a sealed container away from light (especially for photoresist)

**Pre-laser inspection:**
- Hold the board to a strong light at a low angle
- Look for thin spots, drips, dust, or fingerprints in the resist
- Any defect here becomes a defect in the final board
- Re-coat or sand and start over if in doubt — five minutes of sanding beats a wasted etch run
requiredTools: Resist material (matte black spray paint, photoresist, etc.)
warnings: Spray paint and acetone fumes are flammable and toxic — work in a well-ventilated area away from ignition sources
Bare fingers transfer oils that cause etchant lift-off. Always handle by edges or wear nitrile gloves
tips: Cure spray paint at least 24 hours, ideally with mild heat (a heated cabinet at 40°C). Under-cured paint smears under the laser
Practice the laser settings on a piece of scrap-coated board first, every time you change batches of paint or board stock
completionCriteria: Surface is uniformly coated with no pinholes, drips, or dust visible at low-angle light
Resist is fully cured (touch test on a corner — no smudge, no fingerprint)
Board has not been touched on the coated face since cleaning

steps.title: Generate the isolation toolpath
steps.description: Use FlatCAM or pcb2gcode to convert the Gerber/SVG into the laser path that ablates resist around traces.
steps.content:
Isolation routing removes the resist (and later, the copper) only around traces, leaving the rest of the copper plane intact. This is the dominant home-PCB technique because it avoids the chemistry, time, and waste of full-area etching.

**FlatCAM workflow (recommended for first-timers):**

FlatCAM is open-source CAM software that reads Gerbers and produces G-code or laser paths. Download from http://flatcam.org.

**Step 1 — Load the Gerber:**
1. **File → Open Gerber** → select `mysplit-v1-B_Cu.gbr` (or your back-copper Gerber)
2. The board renders in the project view
3. Confirm dimensions and orientation

**Step 2 — Generate the isolation geometry:**
1. Select the Gerber object in the Project tab
2. **Selected → Isolation Routing**
3. **Tool diameter:** set to your laser kerf — typically **0.1-0.2mm** for diode lasers. Measure your kerf on a scrap test piece if uncertain
4. **Passes:** 2-4. More passes = wider isolation channel = more reliable separation but more laser time. Start with 2
5. **Pass overlap:** 25-50%. Higher overlap = smoother edges
6. **Combine passes:** ON
7. **Generate Geometry**

**Step 3 — Convert geometry to a laser job:**
1. Select the new geometry object
2. **Selected → CNC Job**
3. **Tool dia:** same as isolation step
4. **Travel Z** and **Cut Z:** for a laser, set both to 0 (the laser is a 2D operation; Z is irrelevant)
5. **Feed rate:** start at 600 mm/min for a 5W diode laser, 1500 mm/min for 20W+. Tune on test pieces
6. **Spindle speed:** the laser power. 100% for resist ablation on most diode lasers
7. **Generate**

**Step 4 — Export G-code:**
1. Select the CNC Job object
2. **Selected → Export G-Code**
3. **Postprocessor:** GRBL_laser (most common for hobby lasers)
4. Save as `mysplit-v1-bcu-iso.gcode`

**pcb2gcode alternative (command-line):**
```
pcb2gcode --back mysplit-v1-B_Cu.gbr \
  --back-output mysplit-v1-bcu.ngc \
  --offset 0.1 \
  --mill-diameters 0.2 \
  --mill-feed 600 \
  --metric \
  --postamble "M5\nG0 X0 Y0\nM30"
```

Faster for repeated runs once you settle on parameters; harder to inspect.

**LightBurn alternative (raster-based):**
If you exported a high-DPI PNG instead of a Gerber:
1. **File → Import** the PNG
2. Set the image to **Threshold** mode (no greyscale)
3. Select the image; create a new layer with **Mode: Fill**
4. Speed: 600-1500 mm/min, Power: 100%
5. Confirm the work envelope matches the board, click **Frame** to trace the outline before firing

**Simulate before burning:**
FlatCAM and LightBurn both have a path simulator. Watch the full job play through. Look for:
- Travel moves crossing copper that should not be cut
- Missed traces (a gap where there should be a path)
- Spurious paths outside the board outline

A single missed isolation pass leaves a copper bridge between traces — short circuit on first power-up.
warnings: A laser kerf wider than the actual cut leaves bridges between traces. Calibrate kerf on a scrap test piece for every new batch of resist
tips: Save FlatCAM project files (`.flatcam_prj`) per board — re-tuning every revision wastes time
Run a 5×5mm test square at full power and feed before the real job. Confirms focus, kerf, and ablation completeness
completionCriteria: G-code or laser job loads in your laser software without errors
Path simulation shows isolation around every trace
Test cut on scrap material confirms full resist removal in the cut path

steps.title: Double-sided alignment
steps.description: Get the front and back copper layers aligned within the laser's tolerance.
steps.content:
Double-sided alignment is the single hardest part of laser PCB making. Misalignment of 0.2mm or more turns vias into dead ends and shifts pads off their components. If this is your first board, **strongly consider redesigning to single-layer with jumper wires** — every hour you save in design pays for itself in successful etches.

**The core problem:**
You laser one side of the board, flip it over, and need to laser the other side at exactly the right position relative to the first side. Drift comes from:
- Movement when flipping
- Slight rotation during re-mounting
- Z-axis variation across the bed
- Thermal expansion of the resist

**The two reliable techniques:**

**Technique 1 — Drilled registration holes (best for separate layers):**

1. In KiCad, add **3 small (1.0mm) holes** on the Edge.Cuts layer at known positions. Place them outside the board outline if possible, otherwise in mounting hole positions. Use 3 (not 2) so orientation cannot be flipped
2. Export the front and back copper SVGs/Gerbers as usual
3. Print the front and back PNG/SVG at 1:1 on regular paper
4. Tape the back-layer print face-up to a flat surface
5. Tape the front-layer print face-down on top, aligned by the registration holes (use a backlight to see through the paper)
6. If they line up on paper, your KiCad design is consistent. If not, the issue is in export (probably mirror direction)
7. Now drill the 3 registration holes through the actual copper-clad board BEFORE coating with resist
8. Build a jig: a flat baseboard with 3 locating pins (1.0mm brass rod or drill bit shanks) at the matching positions. The board drops onto the jig in exactly one orientation
9. Laser side 1, lift, flip the board, drop onto the jig flipped. Laser side 2

**Technique 2 — Book / fold-over (double-sided in one pass):**

For small boards (under ~50mm), you can laser both sides without unmounting:
1. Tape a sheet of paper or thin cardboard to the laser bed as a sacrificial layer
2. Place the coated copper-clad board on the bed; tape one edge firmly
3. Laser the front (top) layer
4. Without moving the laser bed coordinates, lift the board, fold it over along the taped edge like a book. The fold becomes a perfect axis of symmetry
5. Re-tape the now-flipped board
6. Laser the back layer using the SAME G-code file (the bed coordinates have not moved; the board has flipped, so the mirroring is automatic)
7. Requires that your KiCad mirror settings are off for both sides (the physical fold does the mirroring)

**Pre-laser alignment verification:**
Before firing the laser, use the laser at 1% power (visible, non-cutting) to "trace" the perimeter of the cut on the board. Hold a piece of white paper above to see where the beam is hitting. If the trace runs off the board edge or skips a registration mark, stop and re-mount.

**After lasering — confirm with a backlight:**
Hold the etched board (before chemical etching) up to a strong light. The two copper patterns should align. Vias should appear as continuous holes from front to back, not crescents.

**Failure mode handling:**
If alignment is off by less than the trace clearance (typically 0.4mm), the board may still work but with reduced via reliability. If off by more, sand off both sides, re-coat, and redo. Do not try to "fix" misaligned isolation passes by lasering more on top — you will only widen the original cuts.
steps.estimatedTime: 30-60 minutes (or skip entirely by going single-layer)
requiredTools: Drill press or hand drill with 1.0mm bit
Backlight or window for visual alignment check
warnings: Single-layer with jumpers is dramatically more reliable than double-sided home etching. Reconsider before committing to double-sided
tips: For boards larger than ~80mm, the fold-over technique fails because the fold axis introduces slight rotation. Use the registration-hole jig instead
Mark which side is "front" with a tiny scratch on the board edge — once both sides are coated and partly burned, they look identical
completionCriteria: Backlit board shows aligned via positions on both sides
Isolation passes on both sides are continuous (no gaps where alignment drifted)
No more than 0.2mm offset between front and back features

steps.title: Etch, drill, and verify
steps.description: Etch unmasked copper, drill through-holes, electrically test the board before populating with components.
steps.content:
After lasering, the board has resist removed only where copper should be removed. The chemistry phase converts that pattern into actual cleared copper.

**Choose an etchant — pros and cons:**

- **Ferric chloride (FeCl₃)** — traditional, slow, brown stains everything, hard to dispose of. Reliable
- **Cupric chloride (CuCl₂)** — regenerable (you make more from used etchant + HCl + peroxide), green-blue, etches faster than FeCl₃
- **Vinegar + hydrogen peroxide + salt** — household chemistry. Slowest, weakest, but disposable. Good for one-off boards
- **Sodium persulfate** — clear solution (you can watch the etch), slow, requires heating

For a first board, **ferric chloride** is the path of least surprise.

**Etch setup:**
1. **Wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses.** All etchants attack skin and eyes
2. **Work in a well-ventilated area** over a sink or a plastic tray with a paper towel base — spills will happen
3. **Pre-warm the etchant** to 35-45°C (in a water bath or on low on a hot plate). Cold etchant works but takes 4× longer
4. **Place the board copper-side-up in a shallow plastic tray** of etchant. The board should be just submerged
5. **Agitate continuously** by gently rocking the tray. Stagnant etchant develops a depleted layer at the copper surface and stops working

**Etch time and monitoring:**
- 1oz copper at 40°C in fresh ferric chloride: 8-15 minutes
- Check every 2-3 minutes by lifting the board out with plastic tweezers and rinsing under water
- The etch is complete when **all** exposed copper is dissolved — no pink or copper-coloured patches remain in the field
- Over-etching for 30-60 seconds beyond visible completion is fine; it slightly under-cuts the resist edges and rounds the trace corners
- Massive over-etching (5+ minutes beyond completion) eats under the resist and narrows your traces below their design width

**Stop and rinse:**
1. Lift the board out, rinse with copious cold water for 30 seconds
2. Dry with paper towel
3. Inspect under bright light — every trace and pad should be cleanly defined with no copper bridges or breaks
4. **If you see bridges:** carefully scrape with a hobby knife or re-etch for 1-2 more minutes
5. **If you see breaks:** repair with a thin solder bridge or a short jumper wire after assembly

**Dispose of used etchant safely:**
- Never down the drain
- Neutralise FeCl₃ with sodium hydroxide (lye) until pH 7, then take to a household hazardous waste facility
- Cupric chloride: regenerate or take to hazardous waste
- Vinegar + peroxide + salt: dilute heavily and dispose per local regulation (still not down the drain — the dissolved copper is toxic)

**Remove the resist:**
- Spray paint: scrub with acetone and a paper towel until copper shines
- Photoresist: use the manufacturer-recommended stripper, often acetone or 5% sodium hydroxide

**Drill through-holes:**
1. Use the drill map PDF as a reference
2. Drill diameters: 0.7mm for diode leads, 0.8-1.0mm for switch through-pins, 1.0-3.0mm for mounting holes
3. A small drill press is far better than a hand drill — even a few degrees of tilt cracks the trace pads
4. Drill from the copper side; the bit exits through the FR4. Back the board with a piece of scrap wood to prevent breakout
5. Take it slowly — these bits are fragile (carbide, often <$0.50 each, but they break with the slightest side load)

**Continuity-test the board BEFORE soldering anything:**
1. Set multimeter to continuity (beep mode)
2. Test every row trace end-to-end
3. Test every column trace end-to-end
4. Test row-to-row and column-to-column — should NOT beep (no shorts)
5. Test row-to-column at every switch position — should NOT beep (open circuit until a switch is pressed)
6. Test power and ground rails for shorts to any signal trace

**Mark and document:**
- Number the board (e.g. write "v1.2 #1" on a non-copper area with permanent marker)
- Photograph both sides for your build log
- Note any hand-repaired bridges or jumpers — they may fail later and you will need to remember where to look
requiredTools: Plastic tray (large enough for the board)
Hot water bath or hot plate (low setting)
Drill press with PCB-suitable carbide bits
warnings: Etchants are corrosive and toxic. Use full PPE and work in a ventilated area. Never pour etchant down a drain
Carbide PCB drill bits snap with even a small side load. Use a press, not a hand drill, where possible
Continuity-test the bare board before soldering. Finding a short after assembling 60 switches turns a 2-minute fix into a 4-hour rework
tips: Save spent ferric chloride in a glass jar for reuse — it loses potency but a few rounds of warming and agitating extend its life by 3-5 boards
For a first board, etch in batch with a known-good test pattern (a comb of 0.4mm and 0.8mm parallel traces). Confirms etchant strength before risking your real board
completionCriteria: All exposed copper is fully cleared
No bridges or breaks in any trace under magnification
All through-holes are clean and the right diameter
Continuity test passes: rows continuous, columns continuous, no row/col shorts, no power/signal shorts

phases.title: ESD Safety & Component Handling
phases.description: Protect your components from electrostatic discharge before handling

steps.title: Electrostatic Discharge Precautions
steps.description: Set up ESD protection before touching any electronic components
steps.content:
Electrostatic discharge (ESD) is invisible but can permanently damage microcontrollers, diodes, LEDs, and OLED displays. A single undetected discharge can cause components to fail days or weeks after assembly. Spend five minutes on ESD precautions now to protect a build worth many hours of effort.

**What is ESD?**
Your body accumulates static charge simply by walking across carpet, pulling a shirt over your head, or sliding in a chair. That charge discharges through any conductive path — including sensitive semiconductor junctions. ICs can be damaged by voltages as low as 100V, well below the ~3,000V you need to feel a shock.

**Setting up an ESD-safe workspace:**
1. **Anti-static wrist strap** — Clip one end to your wrist and the other to an unpainted metal surface (chassis of a desktop PC, metal workbench, or a purpose-built ground point). This is the single most effective precaution
2. **Anti-static mat** — Place a conductive mat on your work surface and connect it to the same ground point. Available cheaply from electronics suppliers
3. **Anti-static bags** — Keep components in their original anti-static packaging until the moment you need them. Never place ICs or PCBs on ordinary plastic bags or Styrofoam
4. **Touch ground frequently** — If you don't have a wrist strap, touch a grounded metal object before picking up every new component
5. **Avoid synthetic clothing** — Natural fibres (cotton) generate less static than polyester or wool. Roll up loose sleeves before leaning over the board
6. **Humidity** — ESD risk is highest in dry winter conditions or in air-conditioned rooms. A humidity level above 40% significantly reduces static build-up

**Handling rules:**
- Always pick up PCBs by their edges — fingertips on traces or component pads transfer oils and can scratch copper
- Never touch microcontroller pins, IC legs, or LED pads with bare fingers unless you are grounded
- When handing a PCB to someone else, both of you should touch the same grounded surface simultaneously before the handoff
- Store unused PCBs and ICs in anti-static bags between sessions

**Minimum viable precaution (if you have no ESD equipment):**
Touch an unpainted metal pipe, radiator, or the metal chassis of a grounded desktop computer before every session, and again any time you leave the chair. This is far better than nothing.
warnings: ESD damage is cumulative and often causes delayed failures — a component may appear to work initially but fail within days
RP2040 and ARM-based microcontrollers are more ESD-sensitive than older AVR chips
Never place OLED modules, RGB LEDs, or hot-swap sockets directly on cardboard or plastic bags
tips: A $5 anti-static wrist strap from any electronics supplier is the best investment for your build
Keep components in their anti-static bags until the exact moment of installation
If you must work without equipment, work quickly and touch ground before picking up each component

phases.title: Build Key Matrix
phases.description: Wire or solder your switches into a matrix

steps.title: Prepare Switches for Handwiring
steps.description: Mount switches in plates and prepare for wiring
steps.content:
Handwiring gives you complete freedom in layout but requires careful planning. Let's get your switches ready.

**Switch mounting:**
1. **Test fit** - Insert a few switches into your plate or case to verify they snap in securely
2. **Plan your layout** - Use keyboard-layout-editor.com to finalize your key positions
3. **Mount all switches** - Press switches firmly into plate until they click. They should be flush and not wobble
4. **Verify alignment** - Look at your keyboard from the side. All switches should be at the same height

**Matrix planning:**
You need to understand how keyboard matrices work:
- Switches are arranged in ROWS and COLUMNS
- Each switch connects one row to one column
- Diodes prevent ghosting and allow n-key rollover
- Typical split keyboard: 3-4 rows, 6-7 columns per half

**Prepare your diodes:**
1. **Check orientation** - Diodes have a cathode (marked with black line) and anode (unmarked end)
2. **Bend leads** - Bend diode legs 90° about 3mm from the body for easier soldering
3. **Sort and organize** - Keep diodes in a container where they won't get mixed up

**Wire preparation:**
- Cut wire into appropriate lengths (add 20% extra for routing flexibility)
- Strip 2-3mm of insulation from wire ends
- Pre-tin stripped ends with a small amount of solder
- Use different colors for rows vs columns (e.g., red for rows, black for columns)
warnings: CRITICAL: Plan your matrix before soldering. Fixing mistakes after is very difficult
Verify switch plate compatibility - some switches only work with specific plate thicknesses
Don't bend switch pins before insertion - this makes removal nearly impossible
tips: Take photos of your switch layout before wiring - you'll reference this constantly
Label rows and columns with painter's tape during assembly
Start with the most accessible row to build confidence

externalLinks.title: Handwiring a Custom Keyboard
externalLinks.description: Detailed photo guide to handwiring process

steps.title: Wire Row Connections
steps.description: Connect switches horizontally using wire
steps.content:
Rows connect all switches in a horizontal line. We'll wire these first, then add columns.

**Wiring strategy:**
Row wiring connects one pin of each switch in a horizontal line. This pin will later connect to a controller GPIO pin.

**Step-by-step process:**
1. **Identify row pins** - Usually the bottom-left or top-left pin of each switch
2. **Route first wire** - String wire from the first switch to the last switch in the row, keeping it taut but not tight
3. **Solder each connection** - Touch iron and solder to the switch pin and wire simultaneously. Hold for 2-3 seconds until solder flows
4. **Inspect joints** - Good solder joints are shiny, smooth, and cone-shaped. Dull or blobby joints indicate cold solder
5. **Trim excess wire** - Cut close to the last switch
6. **Repeat for all rows** - Work methodically row by row

**Quality checkpoints:**
- Each solder joint should be mechanically strong (tug gently to test)
- Wire routing should be clean and organized
- No solder bridges between adjacent pins
- No exposed wire that could short to other connections

**Troubleshooting common issues:**
- **Cold solder joint (dull gray):** Reheat and add a tiny bit more solder
- **Too much solder (blob):** Use solder wick to remove excess
- **Solder won't stick:** Clean the tip, add flux, try again
warnings: Double-check which pin you're using for rows - mixing pins will break your matrix
Keep wires away from plate edges where they might get pinched during case assembly
Let each joint cool completely before moving to the next
tips: Work in good lighting - bad solder joints are easier to spot immediately
Clean your iron tip every 5-10 joints
Use flux if solder isn't flowing smoothly
Take breaks - fatigue leads to mistakes

steps.title: Install Diodes on Row Wires
steps.description: Solder diodes to enable n-key rollover
steps.content:
Diodes are essential for proper keyboard function. They prevent ghosting and allow you to press multiple keys simultaneously.

**Understanding diode orientation:**
This is the #1 mistake in handwired builds. Diodes MUST be oriented correctly:
- **Cathode (black line)** connects to the row wire you just soldered
- **Anode (plain end)** connects to the switch column pin
- ALL diodes in your entire keyboard should point the same direction

**Installation process:**
1. **Verify orientation** - Look at the first diode. Black line should point toward the row wire
2. **Attach cathode to row** - Wrap or solder the cathode (black line end) to the row wire
3. **Position anode** - The anode (other end) should point toward the switch's column pin
4. **Solder both ends** - Ensure good mechanical and electrical connection
5. **Verify with multimeter** - In diode mode, meter should beep in only one direction
6. **Repeat for every switch**

**Working efficiently:**
- Do all diodes in one row before moving to the next
- Keep your orientation consistent (e.g., all cathodes pointing right)
- Test every 5th diode with multimeter to catch orientation errors early

**Visual check:**
When done, all diodes should:
- Point the same direction
- Have shiny solder joints
- Not touch any other wires or components
- Be mechanically secure
warnings: CRITICAL: Wrong diode orientation is hard to troubleshoot later. Test frequently!
Verify orientation on EVERY diode - even experienced builders make mistakes
Don't assume all diodes from one batch are marked the same way
tips: Use a multimeter in diode mode to verify orientation before soldering
Mark the cathode side with a Sharpie on your workbench as a reference
Take a photo of the first row - use it as reference for consistency
Pre-bend all diodes before starting for faster assembly

externalLinks.description: Visual explanation of diode function and orientation

steps.title: Wire Column Connections
steps.description: Complete the matrix by wiring columns
steps.content:
Column wiring completes your keyboard matrix. Each column connects vertically through the diodes.

**Column wiring connects through diodes:**
Unlike rows (which connected directly to switches), columns connect to the diode anodes. This completes the matrix circuit.

**Installation process:**
1. **Identify column path** - Follow the vertical line of diode anodes
2. **Route wire** - Run wire vertically from top to bottom of the column
3. **Solder to each diode anode** - Connect wire to the diode's plain end (not the black line end)
4. **Keep wire taut** - Prevents tangling and shorts
5. **Verify no shorts** - Use multimeter to check no columns are shorted together
6. **Repeat for all columns**

**Matrix testing:**
Before connecting to the controller, test your matrix:
1. **Continuity test rows** - Each row should have continuity across all switches
2. **Continuity test columns** - Each column should show continuity through diodes (one direction only)
3. **No shorts between rows** - Adjacent rows should NOT have continuity
4. **No shorts between columns** - Adjacent columns should NOT have continuity

**Common issues:**
- **Short circuits:** Usually caused by loose wire strands or solder bridges
- **Open circuits:** Cold solder joints or broken wires
- **Inconsistent results:** Intermittent connections from mechanical stress

**Documentation:**
Create a matrix map showing:
- Which row wire goes to which controller pin (document for later)
- Which column wire goes to which controller pin
- Take a photo of your finished matrix
warnings: Test the matrix BEFORE connecting to controller - shorts can damage the controller
Don't skip continuity testing - finding problems now saves hours later
Label each row and column wire - you'll need this for firmware configuration
tips: Use different colored wire for each column to simplify troubleshooting
Create a wiring diagram as you go - your future self will thank you
Test each column immediately after wiring it
Strain relief: add a drop of hot glue where wires might flex

externalLinks.title: Matrix Testing Guide
externalLinks.description: QMK documentation on handwiring and testing

steps.title: Inspect PCB Kit Components
steps.description: Verify PCB quality and identify components
steps.content:
PCB kits simplify assembly, but you should still inspect everything before soldering.

**PCB inspection:**
1. **Visual check** - Look for cracks, scratches, or manufacturing defects
2. **Check traces** - Ensure no broken traces or lifted pads
3. **Verify holes** - All through-holes should be clean and open
4. **Test continuity** - Use multimeter to verify key traces if you have the schematic

**Component identification:**
Your kit should include:
- 2x PCBs (left and right halves)
- Diodes (usually SMD or through-hole, pre-counted)
- Resistors (if needed for certain features)
- TRRS jacks or wireless components
- Reset button
- Controller sockets or controller itself

**Organize before starting:**
1. **Separate by type** - Diodes in one container, resistors in another
2. **Verify quantities** - Count components against kit manifest
3. **Read kit instructions** - Many kits have specific assembly orders
4. **Identify orientation markers** - Note any polarity markings on PCB

**Assembly order (typical):**
Most PCB kits follow this sequence:
1. SMD components (if any) - resistors, capacitors
2. Diodes (observe polarity!)
3. Controller socket or controller
4. Reset button and TRRS jack
5. Switches or hot-swap sockets
6. Testing
7. Optional features
warnings: Don't assume the kit is complete - verify everything before starting
Some PCBs have top and bottom sides marked - verify before soldering
Follow the kit's specific instructions if they differ from this guide
tips: Take photos of the PCB before starting in case you need to reference later
Use a magnifying glass or phone camera to inspect SMD pads
Test the PCB with a multimeter if you're unsure about its condition

steps.title: Solder Diodes to PCB
steps.description: Install diodes following PCB markings
steps.content:
Diodes on PCBs are easier than handwiring, but orientation is still critical.

**Diode types:**
Your PCB will have either:
- **Through-hole (THT):** Legs go through holes, easy for beginners
- **Surface mount (SMD):** Tiny components soldered to pads, requires steady hands

**Through-hole diode installation:**
1. **Find orientation marker** - PCB will have a line or symbol matching the diode's cathode (black line)
2. **Bend leads** - 90° bend matching hole spacing
3. **Insert diode** - Cathode line matches PCB marking (usually a white line or square pad)
4. **Flip PCB** - Diodes on top, you solder from bottom
5. **Solder joints** - Heat pad and lead together, apply solder, remove iron
6. **Trim leads** - Cut close to PCB with flush cutters
7. **Verify orientation** - Double-check every diode before moving on

**SMD diode installation:**
1. **Apply solder to one pad** - Just a tiny amount
2. **Position diode** - Cathode marker (line) matches PCB marking
3. **Tack one end** - Reheat solder blob, slide diode into place with tweezers
4. **Solder other end** - Apply iron and solder to opposite pad
5. **Reflow first joint** - Apply more solder to first side
6. **Inspect** - Diode should be flat, both sides soldered

**Testing diodes:**
Use multimeter in diode mode:
- Should conduct in one direction (shows ~0.5-0.7V)
- Should NOT conduct in reverse (shows OL or infinity)
- If conducts both ways: solder bridge
- If conducts neither way: bad solder joint or dead diode
warnings: CRITICAL: Diode orientation must match PCB markings. Wrong orientation = keyboard won't work
SMD diodes are tiny and easy to lose - work over a container
Don't overheat SMD components - max 2-3 seconds per joint
tips: Do all diodes in one row, then test that row before moving on
For SMD: use flux pen for easier soldering
Take a break every 20-30 minutes to prevent eye strain
Use magnification (jeweler's loupe or phone camera) for SMD work

externalLinks.title: SMD Soldering Tutorial
externalLinks.description: Techniques for soldering small surface mount components

steps.title: Install Switches or Hot-Swap Sockets
steps.description: Mount switches to complete the matrix
steps.content:
The final step in building your key matrix is installing switches.

**Two approaches:**

**A) Hot-swap sockets (no soldering per switch):**
1. **Identify socket pads** - Two pads per switch position
2. **Apply solder to pads** - Tin each pad with a small amount of solder
3. **Position socket** - Metal contacts should align with pads
4. **Solder contacts** - Heat pad and socket contact simultaneously, let solder flow
5. **Verify alignment** - Socket should be flat and straight
6. **Test with switch** - Insert switch to verify it clicks in securely
7. **Repeat for all positions**
8. **Insert all switches** - After all sockets installed, press switches in

**B) Direct solder switches:**
1. **Test fit switches** - Verify they fit PCB holes without force
2. **Insert switches** - Start with corner switches to align PCB and plate
3. **Check alignment** - All switches should be perpendicular to PCB
4. **Solder two pins** - One on opposite corners to hold alignment
5. **Check again** - Make sure switches are flush and straight
6. **Solder remaining pins** - Work systematically
7. **Inspect all joints** - Shiny, smooth, cone-shaped

**Quality checkpoints:**
- Switches are all at same height
- No wobble when pressed
- Pins fully soldered (or hot-swap sockets fully seated)
- No solder bridges between adjacent pads

**Final matrix test:**
Before connecting controller:
1. Use multimeter to verify each switch connects its row and column when pressed
2. Check for shorts between adjacent switches
3. Document any issues for troubleshooting
warnings: Switches must be fully seated before soldering - check from the side
Hot-swap sockets require less solder than you think - don't overdo it
If plate and PCB don't align, do NOT force switches - check for interference
tips: Install corner switches first to align plate and PCB
For hot-swap sockets: test with one switch before doing all positions
Clean PCB with isopropyl alcohol after soldering to remove flux residue
Label the PCB halves (LEFT/RIGHT) before testing

phases.title: PCB Inspection & Continuity Testing
phases.description: Inspect solder work and verify electrical continuity before firmware flash

steps.title: Visual Inspection of All Solder Joints
steps.description: Examine every joint for cold solder, bridges, and damaged pads before powering on
steps.content:
A thorough visual inspection now costs you 20 minutes. Discovering a shorted joint after you have flashed firmware and assembled the case costs you hours. Work methodically under good lighting and magnification.

**What a good solder joint looks like:**
- Shiny, smooth, concave fillet (volcano shape around the lead or pad)
- Adheres cleanly to both the pad and the component leg
- No dull grey or grainy texture (indicates a cold joint)
- No cracks at the base of the fillet
- No whisker-like spikes (indicates too-hot iron or contaminated tip)

**Inspecting for cold solder joints:**
1. Place the PCB under a bright LED desk lamp at a low angle — this creates shadows that make dull, grainy joints obvious
2. Work row by row; inspect every diode, every switch pin, every TRRS jack pin, and every controller header
3. Mark any suspicious joints with a small piece of blue painter's tape
4. Return to marked joints and reflow: apply fresh flux, touch the iron for 2-3 seconds, feed a tiny amount of fresh solder if needed, remove iron cleanly
5. Inspect reflowed joints again before removing the tape marker

**Inspecting for solder bridges:**
A bridge is a small blob of solder connecting two adjacent pads or pins that should be electrically separate. Bridges are especially common:
- On SMD diodes where pads are very close together
- On controller header pins where solder wicks between adjacent pins
- On hot-swap socket pads

To find bridges:
1. Use a jeweller's loupe (10×) or hold your phone camera 5cm away and zoom in
2. Look along the row of pins from the side — bridges appear as a tiny horizontal blob
3. Remove bridges with solder wick: apply flux, lay wick over the bridge, press with iron for 2-3 seconds, lift wick and iron together

**Inspecting for damaged traces:**
1. Look for scratches, cuts, or lifted pads — especially near areas where you used flush cutters to trim leads
2. A lifted pad appears as a copper disc separated from the PCB surface — the fibreglass underneath will be visible
3. Damaged traces can sometimes be repaired with a short wire bridge; lifted pads are harder to fix

**Check component orientation (final pass):**
- All diodes: cathode stripe matches PCB silkscreen marker direction
- TRRS jack: verify correct footprint (some kits have both PJ-320A and Alps/Kailh variants on same board)
- Controller: if socketed, pins aligned correctly before insertion
warnings: Never skip visual inspection — it is the fastest way to catch most assembly errors
Inspect both sides of a double-sided PCB; through-hole leads soldered on the back can still bridge on the front
Do not power on the PCB until continuity testing is complete
tips: A USB desk microscope ($15-30) transforms SMD inspection — highly recommended for future builds
Good lighting matters more than magnification for most inspection tasks
Photograph problem areas with your phone camera; zoomed-in photos often reveal details invisible to the naked eye
requiredTools: Jeweller's loupe or phone camera for magnification

externalLinks.description: Photo guide to identifying good and bad solder joints

steps.title: Continuity Testing on Key Pads
steps.description: Use a multimeter to verify electrical continuity through every switch position
steps.content:
Visual inspection catches physical defects; continuity testing catches electrical ones. These two tests together eliminate the vast majority of assembly faults before firmware is ever involved.

**Multimeter setup:**
Set your multimeter to continuity mode (the mode that beeps when a circuit is closed — usually marked with a diode symbol and a sound-wave icon). If your meter lacks a beeper, use the lowest resistance range and look for a reading near 0Ω.

**Testing individual switch positions:**
For each switch position in turn:
1. Place one probe on the row pad (the pad connected to the row trace, which connects through the diode)
2. Place the other probe on the column pad (the pad connected directly to the column trace)
3. Press and hold the switch
4. The meter should beep (continuity) when the switch is pressed and be silent (open circuit) when released
5. If it beeps in both states: solder bridge, or switch contacts welded
6. If it never beeps: cold joint on switch pin, missing diode, or broken trace

**Testing diode direction:**
1. Place red probe (+) on the anode side of the diode (pad without the cathode stripe on the silkscreen)
2. Place black probe (-) on the cathode side (pad with the stripe)
3. Should beep or show low resistance (forward biased)
4. Swap probes — should NOT beep (reverse biased)
5. If it beeps in both directions: diode is shorted or replaced by a solder bridge
6. If it never beeps: open circuit — check solder joints on both pads

**Testing row and column traces:**
1. Touch both probes to the two ends of each row trace (between the first and last switch pad in that row)
2. Should show continuity (low resistance)
3. Repeat for each column trace
4. Then test each row against every other row — should NOT show continuity
5. Test each column against every other column — should NOT show continuity

**Testing controller connections (if controller is already installed):**
1. One probe on the controller GPIO pin header (or test pad)
2. Other probe at the corresponding row or column trace endpoint
3. Should show continuity for every pin you have wired

**Documenting your results:**
Create a simple grid (photo or sketch) and mark each position:
- Tick: passes switch test
- X: fails switch test (investigate)
- D: diode fault (wrong orientation or open)
- B: solder bridge found and fixed
warnings: Always disconnect from USB before probing — a live board can give false continuity readings and risks short-circuit damage
Pressing too hard with probes can scratch pads or lift them — use gentle contact
A failed diode test in both directions (always open) may indicate a completely missing diode or a cold joint on both pads
tips: Work through the matrix in a fixed order (top-left to bottom-right) to avoid missing positions
If an entire row or column fails, test the controller solder joint for that pin first — one bad joint explains every failure in that line
Keep a tally of faults found and fixed; if you find more than 3-4, do a full re-inspection rather than spot fixes
requiredTools: Fine-tipped probes (hook probes are ideal for PCB work)
Grid sketch or photo of PCB layout for recording results
